fields.subnational_unit: Jinotega and Matagalpa departments (central-north Nicaragua): eight municipalities, 28 communities
fields.sample_size: 417 rural households (7 to 29 polled per community) and structured interviews with the 28 community water committees (CAPS) of 28 communities in 8 municipalities of two departments (Jinotega and Matagalpa), taken from a national study by ONGAWA and the Coalition for the Right to Water (CODA, 2009) that polled 1,350 rural households and 61 CAPS countrywide (CAPS supply about 1,200,000 people); how households were chosen within communities is not described in this paper
fields.effect_measure: composite right-to-water index: 18 indicators in six criteria (availability, physical accessibility, affordability, quality and safety, non-discrimination, participation and access to information), each scored 0-1 from household and committee data and aggregated multiplicatively (non-compensatory) with weights from principal component analysis; descriptive, no estimate of an institutional effect
fields.effect_estimate: Mean criterion scores over the 417 households (Table 3): availability 0.638, physical accessibility 0.794, affordability 0.418, quality and safety 0.659, non-discrimination 0.300, participation and access to information 0.481; composite index 0.216. 279 of the 417 households had a composite index below 0.10 because the multiplicative aggregation gives a very low value when any one criterion fails (Table 4). Piped water was the norm, so quantity was seldom the problem; non-discrimination was the weakest criterion, with affordability and participation also critical. Differences between municipalities and communities are large (in four San Sebastian de Yali communities the composite index ranged from about 0 to 0.64, Figure 3). The authors conclude that a right-to-water measure shows disparities that coverage statistics (JMP improved versus unimproved) hide, that it would sharply lower reported 'coverage', and that the fieldwork itself raised rights awareness and fed advocacy; income, personal security and water quality were hard to measure locally.
fields.section: Full text (journal article, 17 pages; scanned image PDF read page by page): Introduction (right to water, monitoring need); Case study (Nicaragua, Table 1); Methodology (indicators, aggregation, weights); Results (Tables 2-4, Figures 2-3); Findings and discussion; Policy implications; Conclusions

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a measurement-method paper that builds a right-to-water composite index from a 417-household survey and 28 water-committee interviews in rural Nicaragua; descriptive, no estimate of a legal or institutional effect; read in full text 2026-10-09.
pdf_note: Flores, Jimenez and Perez-Foguet 2013 (Int J Water Resources Development 29(4)), 17-page scanned image PDF with no text layer (Drive file 'content (2).pdf'), read page by page as images; the table values were read from the page images, not machine-extracted
notes: ELIGIBILITY NOTE: like S285 (same research group, same Nicaraguan study, a different paper) this tests a measurement method; its link to legal or institutional barriers is the right-to-water framing and the committee-managed (CAPS) supply. The households of S285 (five communities of San Sebastian de Yali, 296 households) and these 417 households come from the same national dataset and probably overlap; not added to the linked-reports file (researcher decision). The MMAT rating was not re-answered: this is mainly a quantitative descriptive index-construction paper, so the tool fit is arguable (decision A11).
